HuYgTa-d1e3XX-d1e111.summary: Opening of Thomas of Strasbourg's inaugural sermon (principium) on the Sentences, taking as its theme Habakkuk 3:10, 'Dedit abyssus vocem suam.' Drawing on Augustine, the Platonists, Dionysius and Anselm, it argues that the rational soul's beatitude consists in union with God alone, but that the soul (pure potency) and God (pure act) are extremes that cannot be joined without a graced, divinely inspired medium. Since the soul in its present darkened state cannot see God directly, it must cling to sacred theology as to God's own 'voice', following that voice through the Scriptures until it can see the beloved face to face. The rightful order to beatitude is thus first to hear God in Scripture, then to see him in his nature (Job 42:5; Ps 47:9), with the student of Scripture first 'liquefied' by the divine word and then transformed into the divine image (Cant 5:6; 2 Cor 3:18).
claims: The rational soul can be beatified only by being united to God, its creator and the giver of beatitude.
Extremes cannot be joined except through a medium; since the soul (pure potency) and God (pure act) are maximally distant, a supernatural, graced medium is required for beatific vision.
By its natural powers in the present state the intellect is to God as the bat's eye is to the sun's light.
In the present life the soul must rely on sacred theology as the 'voice' of God in order to seek him.
The right order to beatitude is first to hear God's voice in Scripture and afterwards to see God in his own nature.
concepts: sacred Scripture as the voice of God

HuYgTa-d1e3XX-d1e374.summary: Summarizes the two conclusions of the opening section — that the soul is beatified only through elevation to the open vision of God, and that it is elevated only by first faithfully following God's voice in the Scriptures — and adds that this voice can be heard only if God speaks. Hence the Father of mercies, out of his own heart, 'uttered a good word' by inspiring the Fathers with Scripture and communicating it in the sacred canon. This, it is claimed, is what Habakkuk signified in the sermon's theme, 'Dedit abyssus vocem suam.'
claims: The soul cannot be blessed unless elevated to the open vision of God.
The soul is not elevated to that vision unless it first faithfully follows God's voice in Scripture.
God's voice can be heard only if God himself speaks; he has done so by inspiring the Fathers with Scripture and communicating it in the canon.
The theme verse Habakkuk 3:10 signifies God's gift of Scripture.

HuYgTa-d1e3XX-d1e418.summary: Announces the division of the sermon: the theme verse will be expounded in two ways, yielding a twofold commendation of Scripture — first Scripture considered universally, as spread out across the Old and New Testaments, and second Scripture as specially gathered and compiled in orderly compendium by Master Peter Lombard in the books of the Sentences.
claims: The theme verse admits a double exposition.
Scripture is commended first as a whole (Old and New Testaments) and second as compiled in the Sentences of Peter Lombard.

HuYgTa-d1e3XX-d1e436.summary: Lays out the first exposition of the theme as a fourfold commendation of Scripture correlated with the four causes. Each word of the verse is mapped to an attribute: 'Dedit' signifies Scripture's copious munificence (efficient cause, its origin in God); 'abyssus' its prodigious eminence (material cause, its subject); 'vocem' its generous luminosity (formal cause, its mode of proceeding); and 'suam' its delightful outflowing that refreshes (final cause). Correspondingly Scripture is marked by inestimable dignity, impenetrable difficulty, unshadowable clarity, and inexhaustible sweetness.
claims: Scripture is commended in four ways corresponding to its efficient, material, formal and final causes.
Each of the four words of Habakkuk 3:10 signifies one of these causes: 'dedit' the originating principle, 'abyssus' the subject, 'vocem' the formal mode of proceeding, 'suam' the final cause.
concepts: dignity, difficulty, clarity and sweetness of Scripture

HuYgTa-d1e3XX-d1e502.summary: Develops the first member of the fourfold commendation: 'Dedit' signifies that God alone is the originating (efficient) principle of Scripture. Since no creature possesses true wisdom (Job 28) and no one gives what he does not have, wisdom must be sought from God alone, as Solomon, James 1:5 and other texts teach. Using an a fortiori argument from Aristotle's remark that metaphysical wisdom is rather a divine than a human possession, the paragraph concludes that this most sacred science depends immediately on God, who must therefore be petitioned in prayer and praised as its giver.
claims: No creature can give true wisdom because no creature possesses it of itself.
Wisdom must be sought from God alone, who gives it abundantly to those who ask.
If even human (metaphysical) wisdom is rightly regarded as a divine possession, a fortiori the sacred science of theology depends immediately on God.
Therefore one must pray devoutly to God for understanding and give him glory for the gift of wisdom.

HuYgTa-d1e3XX-d1e615.summary: Develops the second member: 'abyssus' signifies Scripture's prodigious eminence with respect to its subject or material cause. The subject matter is so deep that it is fittingly compared to an abyss; divine clarity, because of its abyssal immensity, is veiled from our eyes by anagogical coverings, as Dionysius and Hugh of St. Victor's commentary explain (weak eyes can look on the sun only when clouded). Only uncreated Wisdom has penetrated this abyss (Ecclus 24), and Paul's 'O altitudo' (Rom 11:33) is analyzed as admiration, its reason, and the confirmation of that reason.
claims: The subject matter of Scripture is so profound that it is rightly called an abyss.
Divine light can be seen by us only when veiled in sacred, anagogical coverings, as weak eyes can look only at a clouded sun.
No creature can fully penetrate the depth of divine wisdom; only uncreated Wisdom has done so.
concepts: accommodation of revelation to human capacity

HuYgTa-d1e3XX-d1e697.summary: Develops the third member: 'vocem' signifies Scripture's generous luminosity, its formal principle of proceeding, by which it illuminates all who diligently follow it. John 12:28 ('I have glorified and will glorify') is read as God's illumination of prophets and patriarchs in the Old Testament and of Christian students in the New. A chain of authorities (Wisdom 6–7, Cassiodorus, Alan of Lille's De planctu naturae, a Gregorian hymn) praises wisdom as unfading light, incorruptible, multiplied by being shared, transforming earthly man into a heavenly and deified one.
claims: Scripture's voice illuminates all those who study and follow it.
Divine wisdom is an unfailing light that is not diminished by time or concealment but multiplied by communication.
Sacred wisdom transforms the earthly human into a heavenly one by a deifying change.

HuYgTa-d1e3XX-d1e785.summary: Develops the fourth member: 'suam' signifies Scripture's delightful, refreshing outflow, its final cause. Since 'suus' is a relative pronoun, it refers the voice back to its origin in God, implying a final cause whose abundant goodness refreshes all things. Citing Isaiah, Augustine's Confessions, Revelation, Jerome on Psalm 147 and Isidore, the paragraph presents the divine word as containing every spiritual delight and, like manna, tasting according to each one's capacity. It closes the first exposition of the theme.
claims: The pronoun 'suam' refers the voice back to God, its source, and thus implies the final cause.
Scripture's end is the refreshment and consolation of the soul.
The divine word contains all spiritual delights and, like manna, adapts its savor to each person's understanding.

HuYgTa-d1e3XX-d1e873.summary: Begins the second exposition of the theme, in which its four words commend the four books of the Sentences: Book I treats the most sublime condition of divine secrets (abyssus), Book II the most sufficient production of all creatures (dedit), Book III the wondrous conjunction of highest and lowest in the Incarnation (vocem), and Book IV the efficacious healing of the infirm by the sacraments (suam). Only the first member is then developed: in Book I 'abyss calls to abyss' — the abyss of essential unity calls to the abyss of personal trinity — a mystery no creature can scrutinize (Hilary, De Trinitate 2), yet God lets droplets of its light flow down to illuminate the intellect and inflame the affections of devout students. The sermon closes with Augustine's (pseudo-Augustinian Soliloquies) prayer to the true light and a concluding doxology.
claims: The four books of the Sentences treat, respectively, the divine secrets (God, One and Three), the production of creatures, the union of God and humanity, and the healing of the infirm.
Each of the four words of the theme commends one book: 'abyssus' Book I, 'dedit' Book II, 'vocem' Book III, 'suam' Book IV.
In Book I the abyss of essential unity is contemplated together with the abyss of personal trinity.
The Trinity cannot be fully penetrated by any mortal, yet God grants partial illumination to devout students.

HuYgTa-d1e3XX.summary: Thomas of Strasbourg's inaugural sermon (principium) commending sacred Scripture and the Sentences on the theme 'Dedit abyssus vocem suam' (Hab 3:10). It first argues that the rational soul's beatitude requires a graced medium, and that in this life that medium is God's 'voice' in Scripture, which must be heard before God can be seen. The theme is then expounded twice: first as a fourfold commendation of Scripture according to its four causes (God as giver, the abyssal subject, its illuminating form, its refreshing end); second as a commendation of the four books of the Sentences (God One and Three, creation, Incarnation, sacraments), of which only the first — the abyss of divine unity and trinity — is developed before a closing prayer for illumination.
claims: Beatitude requires a supernatural medium joining the soul to God, and in this life that medium is Scripture as God's voice.
Scripture is commended according to its efficient, material, formal and final causes.
The four books of the Sentences are commended through the four words of the theme verse.
